claim: Bacteria regulate their metabolism to adapt and survive adverse conditions, in particular to stressful downshifts in nutrient availability.
source: Bacteria regulate their metabolism to adapt and survive adverse conditions, in particular to stressful downshifts in nutrient availability.
evidence: This is a general statement about bacterial physiology that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Stressful downshifts in nutrient availability trigger the stringent response, coordinated by the signaling molecules guanosine tetra and pentaphosphate collectively referred to as (p)ppGpp.
source: These shifts trigger the so-called stringent response, coordinated by the signaling molecules guanosine tetra and pentaphosphate collectively referred to as (p)ppGpp.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about the stringent response mechanism.

claim: In Escherichia coli, accumulation of (p)ppGpp depends on the (p)ppGpp synthetase RelA and the bifunctional (p)ppGpp synthetase/hydrolase SpoT.
source: In Escherichia coli, accumulation of theses alarmones depends on the (p)ppGpp synthetase RelA and the bifunctional (p)ppGpp synthetase/hydrolase SpoT.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about (p)ppGpp metabolism in E. coli.

claim: NirD restrains RelA-dependent accumulation of (p)ppGpp in E. coli.
source: In this study, we show that the small protein NirD restrains RelA-dependent accumulation of (p)ppGpp and can inhibit the stringent response in E. coli.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: NirD can inhibit the stringent response in E. coli.
source: In this study, we show that the small protein NirD restrains RelA-dependent accumulation of (p)ppGpp and can inhibit the stringent response in E. coli.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: NirD directly binds the catalytic domains of RelA to balance (p)ppGpp accumulation.
source: Mechanistically, our in vivo and in vitro studies reveal that NirD directly binds the catalytic domains of RelA to balance (p)ppGpp accumulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in vivo and in vitro experimental data.

claim: NirD can control RelA activity by directly inhibiting the rate of (p)ppGpp synthesis.
source: Finally, we show that NirD can control RelA activity by directly inhibiting the rate of (p)ppGpp synthesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in vitro experimental data.

claim: The stringent response is a general stress response mediated by the accumulation of ppGpp and pppGpp.
source: Among these signaling pathways, the stringent response is a general stress response that is mediated by the accumulation of the nucleotides guanosine 5′-diphosphate 3′-diphosphate (ppGpp) and guanosine 5′-triphosphate 3′-diphosphate (pppGpp), collectively known as (p)ppGpp (Potrykus and Cashel, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: (p)ppGpp allows bacteria to rapidly respond and adapt to various conditions of nutritional and environmental stress by affecting gene expression and metabolism.
source: These alarmones allow bacteria to rapidly respond and adapt to various conditions of nutritional and environmental stress by affecting gene expression and metabolism.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about (p)ppGpp function.

claim: In Gram-negative bacteria, (p)ppGpp binds RNA polymerase, thereby altering its promoter selectivity, which results in genome-wide transcriptional reprograming.
source: In Gram-negative bacteria, (p)ppGpp binds RNA polymerase, thereby altering its promoter selectivity, which results in genome-wide transcriptional reprograming (Durfee et al., 2008; Ross et al., 2013; Ross et al., 2016; Sanchez-Vazquez et al., 2019; Traxler et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: (p)ppGpp binds directly and alters the activity of several enzymes including DNA primase, translation factors, lysine decarboxylase, and polyphosphate kinase.
source: Additionally, (p)ppGpp also binds directly and alters the activity of several enzymes including DNA primase, translation factors, lysine decarboxylase, and polyphosphate kinase (Corrigan et al., 2016; Kanjee et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2019a; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The rewiring of cell physiology by (p)ppGpp plays a critical role in the regulation of bacterial virulence, survival during host invasion, and antibiotic resistance and tolerance.
source: Importantly, this rewiring of cell physiology also appears to play a critical role in the regulation of bacterial virulence, survival during host invasion, and antibiotic resistance and tolerance (Hauryliuk et al., 2015; Hengge, 2020; Irving et al., 2021; Potrykus and Cashel, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: In Escherichia coli, (p)ppGpp synthesis and hydrolysis are regulated by RelA and SpoT, which are members of RelA/SpoT homologue (RSH) enzymes.
source: In Escherichia coli, (p)ppGpp synthesis and hydrolysis are regulated by RelA and SpoT, which are members of RelA/SpoT homologue (RSH) (Atkinson et al., 2011) enzymes and share similar domain architecture.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and draws from established knowledge.

claim: RelA and SpoT share similar domain architecture.
source: In Escherichia coli, (p)ppGpp synthesis and hydrolysis are regulated by RelA and SpoT, which are members of RelA/SpoT homologue (RSH) (Atkinson et al., 2011) enzymes and share similar domain architecture.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about RSH enzyme structure.

claim: The enzymatic N-terminal half (NTD) of RelA and SpoT has the synthetase (SYN) and the hydrolase (HYD) domains.
source: The enzymatic N-terminal half (NTD) has the synthetase (SYN) and the hydrolase (HYD) domains, and the C-terminal half (CTD) of the protein contains conserved domains, which play a critical role in sensing and transducing stress signals to the catalytic domains (Gratani et al., 2018; Hauryliuk et al., 2015; Hogg et al., 2004; Mechold et al., 2002; Pausch et al., 2020; Takada et al., 2020; Tamman et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and draws from established knowledge.

claim: The C-terminal half (CTD) of RelA and SpoT contains conserved domains which play a critical role in sensing and transducing stress signals to the catalytic domains.
source: The enzymatic N-terminal half (NTD) has the synthetase (SYN) and the hydrolase (HYD) domains, and the C-terminal half (CTD) of the protein contains conserved domains, which play a critical role in sensing and transducing stress signals to the catalytic domains (Gratani et al., 2018; Hauryliuk et al., 2015; Hogg et al., 2004; Mechold et al., 2002; Pausch et al., 2020; Takada et al., 2020; Tamman et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: SpoT is a bifunctional enzyme with both hydrolytic and synthetic activities.
source: SpoT is a bifunctional enzyme with both hydrolytic and synthetic activities while RelA is a monofunctional (p)ppGpp synthetase.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about SpoT function.

claim: RelA is a monofunctional (p)ppGpp synthetase.
source: SpoT is a bifunctional enzyme with both hydrolytic and synthetic activities while RelA is a monofunctional (p)ppGpp synthetase.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about RelA function.

claim: RelA maintains a 'pseudo'-hydrolase domain that is structurally conserved but enzymatically inactive.
source: Indeed, despite close sequence similarity between RelA and SpoT, RelA maintains a 'pseudo'-hydrolase domain that is structurally conserved but enzymatically inactive.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about RelA structure.

claim: Activation of the (p)ppGpp synthetase RelA occurs via a ribosomal mechanism in response to amino acid starvation.
source: Activation of the (p)ppGpp synthetase RelA occurs via a ribosomal mechanism in response to amino acid starvation or other stressful conditions, which ultimately result in amino acid starvation, for example, fatty acid starvation, that leads to lysine starvation (Haseltine and Block, 1973; Sinha et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Under amino acid starvation conditions, deacylated tRNAs accumulate and RelA interacts with uncharged tRNA at the vacant ribosomal A-site causing the activation of its (p)ppGpp synthetic activity.
source: Under this condition, deacylated tRNAs accumulate and RelA interacts with uncharged tRNA at the vacant ribosomal A-site causing the activation of its (p)ppGpp synthetic activity (Arenz et al., 2016; Brown et al., 2016; Loveland et al., 2016; Winther et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: RelA is suggested to be inhibited by intra- and/or inter-molecular interactions under replete conditions.
source: Inversely, RelA is suggested to be inhibited by intra- and/or inter-molecular interactions under replete conditions (Gropp et al., 2001; Turnbull et al., 2019; Yang and Ishiguro, 2001), even though it retains residual activity (Murray and Bremer, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: RelA retains residual activity under replete conditions.
source: Inversely, RelA is suggested to be inhibited by intra- and/or inter-molecular interactions under replete conditions (Gropp et al., 2001; Turnbull et al., 2019; Yang and Ishiguro, 2001), even though it retains residual activity (Murray and Bremer, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The hydrolysis function of SpoT provides an opposing activity that is crucial for balancing the basal activity of RelA.
source: Importantly, the hydrolysis function of SpoT provides an opposing activity that is crucial for balancing the basal activity of RelA.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about SpoT function.

claim: Disruption of the spoT gene results in a toxic accumulation of (p)ppGpp and is therefore lethal.
source: Indeed, disruption of the spoT gene results in a toxic accumulation of (p)ppGpp and is therefore lethal (Xiao et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The regulation of SpoT activities involves sources of nutritional stress other than amino acid starvation, including deficiency of fatty acid, phosphate, carbon, and iron.
source: The regulation of SpoT activities involves sources of nutritional stress other than amino acid starvation. These include the deficiency of fatty acid (Seyfzadeh et al., 1993), phosphate (Spira et al., 1995), carbon (Xiao et al., 1991), and iron (Vinella et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: During fatty acid starvation, the accumulation of (p)ppGpp required a specific interaction between the acyl carrier protein and SpoT.
source: During fatty acid starvation, the accumulation of (p)ppGpp required a specific interaction between the acyl carrier protein and SpoT (Battesti and Bouveret, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The binding of the protein YtfK with the catalytic domains of SpoT triggers (p)ppGpp accumulation during phosphate or fatty acid starvation.
source: Similarly, the binding of the protein YtfK with the catalytic domains of SpoT triggers (p)ppGpp accumulation during phosphate or fatty acid starvation (Germain et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Stimulation of the SpoT hydrolase activity is driven through direct interaction with the anti-σ70 factor Rsd upon carbon downshift.
source: In addition, stimulation of the SpoT hydrolase activity is driven through direct interaction with the anti-σ70 factor Rsd upon carbon downshift (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Overproduction of NirD decreases intracellular levels of (p)ppGpp.
source: We thereby discovered that overproduction of NirD, the small subunit of the nitrite reductase, decreases intracellular levels of (p)ppGpp.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Overexpression of nirD limits RelA-dependent accumulation of (p)ppGpp in vivo.
source: Importantly, our results show that overexpression of nirD limits RelA-dependent accumulation of (p)ppGpp in vivo and can prevent activation of the stringent response during amino acid starvation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Overexpression of nirD can prevent activation of the stringent response during amino acid starvation.
source: Importantly, our results show that overexpression of nirD limits RelA-dependent accumulation of (p)ppGpp in vivo and can prevent activation of the stringent response during amino acid starvation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: NirD is not involved in (p)ppGpp breakdown.
source: Moreover, our results show that NirD is not involved in (p)ppGpp breakdown.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: At high concentrations, (p)ppGpp becomes a potent inhibitor of bacterial cell growth.
source: At high concentrations, (p)ppGpp becomes a potent inhibitor of bacterial cell growth.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about (p)ppGpp toxicity.

claim: Overexpression of the relA gene inhibits E. coli growth in amino acid-rich media.
source: Indeed, rising (p)ppGpp levels by overexpression of the relA gene has been shown to inhibit E. coli growth in amino acid-rich media (Schreiber et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The genetic screen identified 88 clones that repetitively grow on non-permissive conditions.
source: This genetic screen led us to identify 88 clones that repetitively grow on non-permissive conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental screen described in the manuscript.

claim: The spoT, gppA, and nirD genes were predominant among the identified genes, with each accounting for almost a third of the genes carried by the sequenced plasmids.
source: The spoT, gppA, and nirD genes were predominant with each one accounting for almost a third of the genes carried by the sequenced plasmids (33.0, 36.4, and 29.5%, respectively) while uhpA was only identified once (1.1%).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental screen described in the manuscript.

claim: uhpA was only identified once in the genetic screen.
source: The spoT, gppA, and nirD genes were predominant with each one accounting for almost a third of the genes carried by the sequenced plasmids (33.0, 36.4, and 29.5%, respectively) while uhpA was only identified once (1.1%).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental screen described in the manuscript.

claim: spoT and gppA revert toxicity associated to (p)ppGpp accumulation.
source: Our observations that spoT and gppA revert toxicity associated to (p)ppGpp accumulation is consistent with previous observations (Germain et al., 2019; Murray and Bremer, 1996; Sanyal and Harinarayanan, 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental screen that is consistent with previous work.

claim: nirD encodes the small subunit of the cytoplasmic nitrite reductase.
source: nirD encodes the small subunit of the cytoplasmic nitrite reductase (Harborne et al., 1992; Peakman et al., 1990a) and has never been linked to the (p)ppGpp metabolism.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: nirD has never been linked to the (p)ppGpp metabolism.
source: nirD encodes the small subunit of the cytoplasmic nitrite reductase (Harborne et al., 1992; Peakman et al., 1990a) and has never been linked to the (p)ppGpp metabolism.
evidence: This statement is based on the absence of previous reports linking nirD to (p)ppGpp metabolism.

claim: NirD can robustly overcome the toxicity associated to (p)ppGpp over-accumulation mediated by RelA.
source: Indeed, as shown in Figure 1B, NirD can robustly overcome the toxicity associated to (p)ppGpp over-accumulation mediated by RelA.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Induction of RelA is associated with a massive accumulation of (p)ppGpp, which is sharply stopped and then decreased upon NirD induction.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, D, induction of RelA is associated with a massive accumulation of (p)ppGpp, which is sharply stopped and then decreased upon NirD induction.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: NirD still suppresses toxicity associated to RelA overproduction when the double expression assay experiment is performed in a ΔrelA spoT background.
source: However, NirD still suppresses toxicity associated to RelA overproduction when the double expression assay experiment is performed in a ΔrelA spoT background (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The hydrolase activity of SpoT is not involved in the reduced (p)ppGpp accumulation observed upon NirD induction.
source: These results show that the hydrolase activity of SpoT is not involved in the reduced (p)ppGpp accumulation observed upon NirD induction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data showing NirD function in a ΔrelA spoT background.

claim: Overexpression of nirD in a ΔrelA strain failed to phenocopy the amino acid auxotrophic characteristic of a ppGpp0 strain.
source: Importantly, overexpression of nirD in a ΔrelA strain failed to phenocopy the well-known amino acid auxotrophic characteristic of a ppGpp0 strain (ΔrelA spoT mutant) (Xiao et al., 1991), strongly arguing that NirD does not act as a small alarmone hydrolase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NirD does not act as a small alarmone hydrolase.
source: Importantly, overexpression of nirD in a ΔrelA strain failed to phenocopy the well-known amino acid auxotrophic characteristic of a ppGpp0 strain (ΔrelA spoT mutant) (Xiao et al., 1991), strongly arguing that NirD does not act as a small alarmone hydrolase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data and inference.

claim: NirD impairs RelA-dependent (p)ppGpp synthesis in E. coli.
source: Taken together, our results show that NirD impairs RelA-dependent (p)ppGpp synthesis in E. coli.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: During amino acid starvation, deacylated tRNAs accumulate and RelA interacts with uncharged tRNA at the vacant ribosomal A-site causing the activation of its (p)ppGpp synthetic activity.
source: Indeed during amino acid starvation, deacylated tRNAs accumulate and RelA interacts with uncharged tRNA at the vacant ribosomal A-site causing the activation of its (p)ppGpp synthetic activity (Arenz et al., 2016; Brown et al., 2016; Loveland et al., 2016; Winther et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: RelA activity is required to survive under amino acid starvation.
source: RelA activity is therefore required to survive under amino acid starvation, and as a result a ΔrelA mutant is not able to grow in the presence of 1 mM serine, methionine, and glycine (SMG), which induces isoleucine starvation (Uzan and Danchin, 1978).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A ΔrelA mutant is not able to grow in the presence of 1 mM serine, methionine, and glycine (SMG), which induces isoleucine starvation.
source: RelA activity is therefore required to survive under amino acid starvation, and as a result a ΔrelA mutant is not able to grow in the presence of 1 mM serine, methionine, and glycine (SMG), which induces isoleucine starvation (Uzan and Danchin, 1978).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Overexpression of nirD in wild-type strain phenocopies the growth defect of a ΔrelA mutant on SMG plate.
source: Interestingly, we observed that overexpression of nirD in wild-type (WT) strain phenocopies the growth defect of a ΔrelA mutant on SMG plate (Figure 2A), suggesting that nirD also prevents (p)ppGpp accumulation from endogenous RelA under these conditions.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: (p)ppGpp rapidly increases in wild-type strain and reaches maximum levels within 5 min after amino acid starvation.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, C, and as previously observed (p)ppGpp rapidly increases in WT strain and reaches maximum levels within 5 min (Cashel and Gallant, 1969).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C, and is consistent with previous work.

claim: When NirD is induced prior to amino acid starvation, no significant accumulation of (p)ppGpp is detected.
source: Remarkably, when NirD is induced prior to amino acid starvation, no significant accumulation of (p)ppGpp is detected (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Once induced, NirD abolishes the stringent response in E. coli.
source: Taken together, our results show that once induced NirD abolishes the stringent response in E. coli.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: Regulation of RSH activities through protein–protein interactions has been previously reported.
source: Regulation of RSH activities through protein–protein interactions has been previously reported (Battesti and Bouveret, 2006; Germain et al., 2019; Hahn et al., 2015; Karstens et al., 2014; Krüger et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2018; Peterson et al., 2020; Raskin et al., 2007; Ronneau et al., 2016; Ronneau et al., 2019; Wout et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: NirD exhibited a strong interaction in vivo with RelA in the bacterial two-hybrid assay.
source: When the E. coli BTH101 strain (cya deficient) is co-transformed with plasmids harboring T18 and T25 fusions, NirD exhibited a strong interaction in vivo with RelA (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No physical interaction is observed between SpoT and NirD in vivo by BTH assay.
source: However, despite the strong sequence homologies between the paralogous RelA and SpoT proteins (Metzger et al., 1989), no physical interaction is observed between SpoT and NirD in vivo by BTH assay (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The NirDE50K mutant displayed compromised interaction with RelA.
source: One of such mutants that had charge reversal amino acid substitution, glutamate 50 to lysine (E50K), displayed compromised interaction with RelA (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Both T18-NirD and T18-NirDE50K recombinant proteins were correctly expressed and folded as shown by their ability to strongly interact with the catalytic subunit of the nitrite reductase NirB.
source: Importantly, we confirm that both T18-NirD and T18-NirDE50K recombinant proteins were correctly expressed and folded as shown by their ability to strongly interact with the catalytic subunit of the nitrite reductase NirB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Harborne et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpression of nirDE50K is not able to suppress toxicity associated to RelA overproduction on plate.
source: Importantly and on the contrary to the results obtained with the WT copy of nirD, we observed that overexpression of nirDE50K is not able to suppress toxicity associated to RelA overproduction on plate (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: nirDE50K failed to stop the massive accumulation of (p)ppGpp observed in vivo after RelA overproduction.
source: Indeed, as shown in Figure 3C, D, nirDE50K failed to stop the massive accumulation of (p)ppGpp observed in vivo after RelA overproduction as compared to the fast decay of (p)ppGpp observed when the WT copy of nirD is expressed (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: nirD is a second gene of a four-gene operon (nirBDC-cysG) strongly induced under anaerobic growth.
source: nirD is a second gene of a four-gene operon (nirBDC-cysG) strongly induced under anaerobic growth (Harborne et al., 1992; Peakman et al., 1990b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ΔnirD mutant presents an extended growth recovery in anaerobic SMG liquid medium consistent with a toxic over-accumulation of (p)ppGpp in this strain.
source: Interestingly, we observed that ΔnirD mutant presents an extended growth recovery in anaerobic SMG liquid medium consistent with a toxic over-accumulation of (p)ppGpp in this strain (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A chromosomal encoded nirDE50K mutant, which is functional for the nitrite reductase activity but failed to interact with RelA, displays the same growth defect as ΔnirD mutant.
source: Indeed, a chromosomal encoded nirDE50K mutant, which is functional for the nitrite reductase activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) but failed to interact with RelA, displays the same growth defect, suggesting that the NirD-RelA interaction is important to adjust proper (p)ppGpp level under this specific growth condition.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The NirD-RelA interaction is important to adjust proper (p)ppGpp level under anaerobic SMG growth condition.
source: Indeed, a chromosomal encoded nirDE50K mutant, which is functional for the nitrite reductase activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) but failed to interact with RelA, displays the same growth defect, suggesting that the NirD-RelA interaction is important to adjust proper (p)ppGpp level under this specific growth condition.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data and inference.

claim: A specific functional interaction between RelA and NirD can lower RelA-dependent accumulation of (p)ppGpp in vivo.
source: Taken together, our results show that a specific functional interaction between RelA and NirD can lower RelA-dependent accumulation of (p)ppGpp in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: RelA consists of several protein domains that have been encompassed in two functional regions, the catalytic NTD and the regulatory CTD.
source: RelA consists of several protein domains that have been encompassed in two functional regions, the catalytic NTD and the regulatory CTD.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about RelA structure.

claim: The N-terminal region of RelA includes the enzymatically inactive (p)ppGpp hydrolase domain (HYD) as well as the functional (p)ppGpp synthetase domain (SYN).
source: The N-terminal region includes the enzymatically inactive (p)ppGpp hydrolase domain (HYD) as well as the functional (p)ppGpp synthetase domain (SYN), while the CTD comprises the Thr-tRNA synthetase, GTPase and SpoT domain (TGS), the alpha helical domain (AH), the zinc finger domain (ZFD), and finally the RNA recognition motif domain (RRM) (Figure 4A) (Brown et al., 2016; Loveland et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and draws from established knowledge.

claim: The CTD of RelA comprises the Thr-tRNA synthetase, GTPase and SpoT domain (TGS), the alpha helical domain (AH), the zinc finger domain (ZFD), and the RNA recognition motif domain (RRM).
source: The N-terminal region includes the enzymatically inactive (p)ppGpp hydrolase domain (HYD) as well as the functional (p)ppGpp synthetase domain (SYN), while the CTD comprises the Thr-tRNA synthetase, GTPase and SpoT domain (TGS), the alpha helical domain (AH), the zinc finger domain (ZFD), and finally the RNA recognition motif domain (RRM) (Figure 4A) (Brown et al., 2016; Loveland et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and draws from established knowledge.

claim: NirD interacts with the RelAN-terminal fusion comprising the catalytic domains.
source: BTH analysis revealed that NirD interacts with the RelAN-terminal fusion comprising the catalytic domains (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: None of the four domains encompassing the CTD of RelA is required for the interaction with NirD in vivo.
source: Moreover, careful quantification of β-galactosidase activity revealed that none of the four domains encompassing the CTD of RelA is required for this interaction in vivo.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Truncated RelA fusion lacking either the synthetase domain (RelA1-181) or the 'pseudo' hydrolase domain (RelA181-744) failed to interact in vivo with NirD.
source: However, truncated RelA fusion lacking either the synthetase domain (RelA1-181) or the 'pseudo' hydrolase domain (RelA181-744) failed to interact in vivo with NirD.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The catalytic domains of RelA seem necessary and sufficient to interact with NirD in vivo.
source: Therefore, the catalytic domains of RelA seem necessary and sufficient to interact with NirD in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data and inference.

claim: The C-terminal region of RelA is proposed to play a key role in the autoregulation of the enzymatic activity.
source: Interestingly, the C-terminal region of RelA is proposed to play a key role in the autoregulation of the enzymatic activity, and as a result the RelAN-terminal truncated protein is constitutively active (Schreiber et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The RelAN-terminal truncated protein is constitutively active.
source: Interestingly, the C-terminal region of RelA is proposed to play a key role in the autoregulation of the enzymatic activity, and as a result the RelAN-terminal truncated protein is constitutively active (Schreiber et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: NirD but not NirDE50K inhibits the toxicity associated with (p)ppGpp over-accumulation mediated by the constitutively active RelAN-terminal.
source: Remarkably, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, we observed that NirD but not NirDE50K inhibits the toxicity associated with (p)ppGpp over-accumulation mediated by the constitutively active RelAN-terminal.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NirD can inhibit RelA activity by interacting with its catalytic N-terminal region in vivo.
source: Taken together, our results show that NirD can inhibit RelA activity by interacting with its catalytic N-terminal region in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: Co-elution of RelAN-terminal and NirD in size-exclusion chromatography resulted in an earlier eluting peak, suggesting the formation of a stable complex.
source: As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, co-elution resulted in an earlier eluting peak, suggesting the formation of a stable complex.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: SDS-PAGE analysis confirmed that RelAN-terminal and NirD were co-eluted from the column.
source: Indeed, SDS-PAGE analysis confirmed that the two proteins were co-eluted from the column (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: NirD directly interacts with the catalytic N-terminal region of RelA as shown by biolayer interferometry.
source: By adding RelA at concentrations ranging from 0.1 to 30 µM, a dose-response association is recorded and decreased during the dissociation step corresponding to the washing of the sensor (Figure 5A), showing that NirD directly interact with the catalytic N-terminal region of RelA.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The dissociation constant (KD) of the NirD-RelAN-terminal interaction is 0.55 µM (± 0.053 µM) as measured by biolayer interferometry.
source: Moreover, by plotting the maximum binding response against the corresponding concentrations of RelA, we calculated a dissociation constant (KD) of 0.55 µM (± 0.053 µM) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: RelAN-terminal did not interact with the NirDE50K variant in vitro by biolayer interferometry.
source: In addition, and in agreement with the BTH assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), RelAN-terminal did not interact with the NirDE50K variant in vitro (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Isothermal titration calorimetry confirmed the direct interaction between NirD and RelAN-terminal with an estimated KD of 0.34 µM.
source: The assay first confirmed the direct interaction between the two proteins with an estimated KD of 0.34 µM (Figure 5B), very similar to that estimated by BLI (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The NirD-RelAN-terminal interaction is a favorable spontaneous exothermic reaction with a ΔH kcal/mol of −3.63 ± 0.208 and is enthalpy driven at 25°C.
source: This reaction is a favorable spontaneous exothermic reaction with a ΔH kcal/mol of −3.63 ± 0.208 and is enthalpy driven at 25°C.
evidence: This is a finding from isothermal titration calorimetry experiments.

claim: No heat exchange was recorded upon titration of RelAN-terminal by NirDE50K in isothermal titration calorimetry.
source: On the contrary and consistent with BLI experiments, no heat exchange was recorded upon titration of RelAN-terminal by NirDE50K, further supporting the strong specificity of the interaction between NirD and RelA (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: NirD interacts directly and specifically with the catalytic domains of RelA in vitro.
source: Collectively, these results show that NirD interacts directly and specifically with the catalytic domains of RelA in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple in vitro experimental findings.

claim: RelAN-terminal protein could efficiently synthetize [32P]-pppGpp in vitro.
source: We observed that RelAN-terminal protein could efficiently synthetize [32P]-pppGpp, but the addition of NirD strongly affected the synthetase activity in vitro.
evidence: This is a finding supported by in vitro experimental data.

claim: The addition of NirD strongly affected the synthetase activity of RelAN-terminal in vitro.
source: We observed that RelAN-terminal protein could efficiently synthetize [32P]-pppGpp, but the addition of NirD strongly affected the synthetase activity in vitro.
evidence: This is a finding supported by in vitro experimental data.

claim: 80% of GTP are converted to pppGpp within 60 min by RelA, whereas only 30% are converted when NirD is added.
source: Indeed, 80% of GTP are converted to pppGpp within 60 min by RelA, whereas only 30% are converted when NirD is added (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Addition of the NirDE50K does not affect the RelA synthetic activity.
source: Importantly, addition of the NirDE50K does not affect the RelA synthetic activity (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: NirD shows a concentration-dependent inhibition of RelA's (p)ppGpp synthetic activity with a half-inhibition occurring at ∼1:1 molar ratio.
source: Finally, careful examination of the initial rates (calculated over the first 150 s) shows a concentration-dependent inhibition of RelA's (p)ppGpp synthetic activity by NirD with a half-inhibition occurring at ∼1:1 molar ratio and a near complete inhibition for the highest tested concentration of NirD (1:16 molar ratio) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: NirD shows near complete inhibition of RelA's (p)ppGpp synthetic activity at 1:16 molar ratio.
source: Finally, careful examination of the initial rates (calculated over the first 150 s) shows a concentration-dependent inhibition of RelA's (p)ppGpp synthetic activity by NirD with a half-inhibition occurring at ∼1:1 molar ratio and a near complete inhibition for the highest tested concentration of NirD (1:16 molar ratio) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: NirD can block pppGpp synthetase activity of RelA through a direct interaction with the catalytic domains.
source: Taken together, these results show that NirD can block pppGpp synthetase activity of RelA through a direct interaction with the catalytic domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: E. coli contains two long RSH enzymes, RelA and SpoT, that synthesize the alarmones (p)ppGpp.
source: E. coli contains two long RSH enzymes, RelA and SpoT, that synthesize the alarmones (p)ppGpp.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about E. coli (p)ppGpp metabolism.

claim: SpoT is the primary source of (p)ppGpp hydrolysis in E. coli.
source: While SpoT is a bifunctional enzyme, RelA is monofunctional with a degenerated hydrolase domain, making SpoT the primary source of hydrolysis (Xiao et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and draws from established knowledge.

claim: A fine-tune regulation of the intracellular (p)ppGpp synthetic and hydrolytic activities in bacteria is crucial to rapidly adjust (p)ppGpp level in response to environmental stress.
source: Therefore, a fine-tune regulation of the intracellular (p)ppGpp synthetic and hydrolytic activities in bacteria is crucial to rapidly adjust (p)ppGpp level in response to environmental stress but also to prevent toxic consequences due to (p)ppGpp over-accumulation (Xiao et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge and is supported by a citation.

claim: NirD constitutes an unprecedented mode of regulation that can prevent accumulation of (p)ppGpp in E. coli.
source: In this study, we uncovered an unprecedented mode of regulation that can prevent accumulation of (p)ppGpp in E. coli.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental findings.

claim: NirD is the small subunit of the cytoplasmic NADH-dependent nitrite reductase complex NirBD.
source: This regulation implicates physical interaction in vivo and in vitro between the catalytic domains of RelA and the protein NirD, the small subunit of the cytoplasmic NADH-dependent nitrite reductase complex NirBD (Harborne et al., 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and draws from established knowledge.

claim: NirD can functionally and directly inhibit the RelA (p)ppGpp synthetic activity.
source: We show that NirD can functionally and directly inhibit the RelA (p)ppGpp synthetic activity.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental findings.

claim: Despite strong sequence homologies and similar domain architecture between RelA and SpoT, no physical interaction was observed between NirD and SpoT.
source: RelA and SpoT are paralogous proteins; however, despite strong sequence homologies and similar domain architecture we were not able to notice physical interaction between NirD and SpoT (Figure 3A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), supporting a specific physiological role of NirD in inhibiting RelA synthetic activity.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: NirD does not seem to lower basal (p)ppGpp level produced by the weak (p)ppGpp synthetase activity encoded by SpoT in the absence of RelA.
source: The absence of a functional link between NirD and SpoT is further reinforced by the observation that NirD does not seem to lower basal (p)ppGpp level produced by the weak (p)ppGpp synthetase activity encoded by SpoT in the absence of RelA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Stimulation of RelA synthetase activity in E. coli is driven by stalled ribosomes upon amino acid starvation.
source: Stimulation of RelA synthetase activity in E. coli is driven by stalled ribosomes upon amino acid starvation (Haseltine and Block, 1973; Wendrich et al., 2002; Winther et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: NtrC-dependent transcription of relA takes an important role in (p)ppGpp accumulation.
source: In addition, NtrC-dependent transcription of relA takes an important role in (p)ppGpp accumulation (Brown et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The identification of NirD as a potent intracellular inhibitor of RelA represents an additional level of complexity in the regulation of the stringent response mediated by RelA.
source: Therefore, the identification of a potent intracellular inhibitor of RelA (p)ppGpp synthetase represents an additional level of complexity in the regulation to the current stringent model mediated by RelA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: The NirD protein level can play an important role for adjusting intracellular (p)ppGpp levels.
source: Our results show that the NirD protein level can play an important role for adjusting intracellular (p)ppGpp levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: Ectopic induction of NirD is sufficient to prevent accumulation of (p)ppGpp mediated by RelA in the absence of nutritional stress.
source: Indeed, ectopic induction of NirD is sufficient to prevent accumulation of (p)ppGpp mediated by RelA in the absence of nutritional stress (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Once expressed, nirD can totally abolish activation of the stringent response during amino acid starvation.
source: Moreover, we show that once expressed, nirD can also totally abolish activation of the stringent response during amino acid starvation (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The estimated concentration of RelA is in the range of 100–400 nM in E. coli.
source: The estimated concentration of RelA is in the range of 100–400 nM in E. coli (Li et al., 2014; Pedersen and Kjeldgaard, 1977).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The NirD-RelA affinity is characterized by a KD in the concentration range of 300–550 nM.
source: Importantly, we found in vitro that the NirD-RelA affinity is characterized by a KD in this concentration range (300–550 nM) (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: At concentrations above the KD, NirD would interact with RelA to catalytically inhibit its activity.
source: Therefore, at concentrations above the KD, NirD would interact with RelA to catalytically inhibit its activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured KD and the mechanism of inhibition.

claim: nirD is maximally induced in the presence of glucose and nitrate under anaerobic growth.
source: nirD is a second gene of a four-gene operon (nirBDC-cysG) expressed under anaerobic growth (Harborne et al., 1992; Peakman et al., 1990b) and maximally induced in the presence of glucose and nitrate (Tyson et al., 1997; Wang and Gunsalus, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Under conditions where nirD is maximally induced, NirD is predicted to reach µM range.
source: Under these conditions, NirD is predicted to reach µM range (Khlebodarova et al., 2016) and regulation of RelA by NirD would therefore become physiologically relevant.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: NirB and NirD can form a stable complex needed for the NADH-dependent nitrite reductase activity.
source: Importantly, while NirB and NirD can form a stable complex needed for the NADH-dependent nitrite reductase activity, we observed that coexpression of nirB and nirD can still counteract RelA-dependent (p)ppGpp accumulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge and is supported by experimental data.

claim: Coexpression of nirB and nirD can still counteract RelA-dependent (p)ppGpp accumulation.
source: Importantly, while NirB and NirD can form a stable complex needed for the NADH-dependent nitrite reductase activity, we observed that coexpression of nirB and nirD can still counteract RelA-dependent (p)ppGpp accumulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The cytoplasmic nitrite reductase NirBD has emerged as a key regulator of the nitric oxide (NO) level during nitrate respiration.
source: The cytoplasmic nitrite reductase NirBD has emerged as a key regulator of the nitric oxide (NO) level during nitrate respiration (Bulot et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: By reducing nitrite generated during nitrate reduction, NirBD would limit the level of toxic nitrite and thus its further reduction to NO.
source: Indeed, by reducing nitrite generated during nitrate reduction, NirBD would limit the level of toxic nitrite and thus its further reduction to NO (Bulot et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: NirD can promote bacterial fitness by adjusting (p)ppGpp levels in response to amino acid starvation under anaerobic glucose fermentation.
source: In addition, our results present evidence that NirD can also promote bacterial fitness by adjusting (p)ppGpp levels in response to amino acid starvation under anaerobic glucose fermentation, a condition where the nitrite reductase is expressed but where the substrate is missing (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The regulation of (p)ppGpp by NirD is dependent on the RelA-NirD interaction.
source: This regulation is dependent on the RelA-NirD interaction since NirDE50K, which is not affected for the nitrite reductase activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) but failed to interact with RelA (Figure 3A), does not enhance bacterial fitness in response to amino acid starvation under anaerobic glucose fermentation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 3E, Figure 3A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: NirD can link (p)ppGpp homeostasis to anaerobic metabolism in E. coli.
source: Therefore, our results suggest that NirD can link (p)ppGpp homeostasis to anaerobic metabolism in E. coli.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: The CTD of RSH enzymes is assumed to play key roles in sensing nutrient starvation and adjusting the enzymatic state of the NTD.
source: The CTD of RSH enzymes is assumed to play key roles in sensing nutrient starvation and adjusting the enzymatic state of the NTD.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about RSH enzyme regulation.

claim: Once bound to the ribosome, RelA adopts an open extended conformation, which is thought to release the autoinhibitory effect of the CTD on the NTD, therefore promoting (p)ppGpp synthesis.
source: In that sense, the RelA structures on stalled ribosomes emphasized the role of CTD in sensing nutrient availability. Once bound to the ribosome, RelA adopts an open extended conformation, which is thought to release the autoinhibitory effect of the CTD on the NTD, therefore promoting (p)ppGpp synthesis (Arenz et al., 2016; Brown et al., 2016; Loveland et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The NTD region of RelA is necessary and sufficient for NirD binding.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the NTD region of RelA is necessary and sufficient for NirD binding (Figure 4B and Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 5.

claim: NirD can inhibit the (p)ppGpp synthesis from the constitutively active truncated RelAN-terminal in vivo and in vitro.
source: Moreover, our in vivo and in vitro results convincingly show that NirD can inhibit the (p)ppGpp synthesis from the constitutively active truncated RelAN-terminal (Figure 6 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), supporting the idea of a ribosome-independent inhibition of the stringent response.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NirD supports a ribosome-independent inhibition of the stringent response.
source: Moreover, our in vivo and in vitro results convincingly show that NirD can inhibit the (p)ppGpp synthesis from the constitutively active truncated RelAN-terminal (Figure 6 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), supporting the idea of a ribosome-independent inhibition of the stringent response.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data and inference.

claim: NirD directly interacts with the catalytic domains of RelA to inhibit the synthetic activity.
source: Therefore, rather than preventing activation of RelA our results support a simple model of regulation in which NirD directly interacts with the catalytic domains of RelA to inhibit the synthetic activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings.

claim: Inhibition of RelA by NirD might be mediated by directly introducing structural changes in the catalytic domains.
source: Such inhibition might be mediated by directly introducing structural changes in the catalytic domains.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of inhibition.

claim: NirD may interact with RelA to avoid nucleotide binding by masking the nucleotide-binding site.
source: Alternatively, NirD may interact with RelA to avoid nucleotide binding by masking the nucleotide-binding site.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of inhibition.

claim: (p)ppGpp has emerged as an important regulator of bacterial stress response, virulence, immune evasion, and antibiotic tolerance.
source: Finally, (p)ppGpp has emerged as an important regulator of not only the bacterial stress response but also of many aspects of bacterial physiology including virulence, immune evasion, and antibiotic tolerance.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about (p)ppGpp function.

claim: Strategies to inhibit RelA activity and the subsequent production of (p)ppGpp represent an attractive approach for the success of antimicrobial therapy.
source: Therefore, strategies to inhibit RelA activity and the subsequent production of (p)ppGpp represent an attractive approach for the success of antimicrobial therapy.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential application of the findings.

claim: There are only a limited number of synthetic inhibitors known to target RelA, mainly based on the design of (p)ppGpp analogues.
source: Currently, there are only a limited number of synthetic inhibitors known to target RelA, mainly based on the design of (p)ppGpp analogues (Wexselblatt et al., 2012; Wexselblatt et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The identification that NirD constitutes a natural potent inhibitor of RelA in vivo and in vitro could represent an important resource for the future design of new drug compounds.
source: Hence, our identification that NirD constitutes a natural potent inhibitor of RelA in vivo and in vitro could represent an important resource for the future design of new drug compounds.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential application of the findings.

claim: NirD is likely to be a fascinating molecular tool to further tackle the functional and structural determinant of the stringent response.
source: Importantly, it is also likely to be a fascinating molecular tool to further tackle the functional and structural determinant of the stringent response.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential application of the findings.
